tagline.text: Everyday Manila eats and halal dishes behind Quiapo Church

location.label: Location
location.text: Quiapo District, Manila (around Plaza Miranda, Hidalgo Street and Carlos Palanca Street)

children.text: Quiapo is the most down-to-earth food district in old Manila. Around Quiapo Church and Plaza Miranda you will find Chinese-Filipino dishes such as palabok, sotanghon and hopia, along with halal dishes from the Muslim quarter. It is a food walk best done slowly and with an eye on your belongings because of pickpockets.

Quiapo is a working-class commercial district in central Manila, where markets, street stalls and old eateries stretch out around Quiapo Church, which draws countless pilgrims. What sets the food apart is that noodle dishes and sweets made by Chinese-Filipinos (Chinoys) and Maranao-style halal dishes from the Muslim quarter sit side by side. Prices are low and portions generous, making it a good place to sample the everyday Filipino table in one go.

The food is concentrated in three areas. The first is the stalls around Plaza Miranda in front of Quiapo Church and along Villalobos Street (fish balls, fried snacks such as kwek-kwek, and dried fish). The second is around Quinta Market on Carlos Palanca Street and under Quezon Bridge (palabok and Chinese-Filipino eateries). The third is the Muslim quarter on A. Bautista Street behind Hidalgo Street (pastil and Maranao dishes). Rather than finishing everything in one place, the trick is to walk slowly through all three and taste one thing in each.

Here are a few signature dishes. Palabok is a Filipino noodle dish of rice noodles topped with a yellow shrimp-broth sauce, crushed chicharon and egg. There are several palabok specialists in Quinta Market and under Quezon Bridge, and some serve a variation topped with squid and lechon kawali (crispy fried pork belly). Sotanghon is a glass-noodle soup, and the noodle shops on Hidalgo Street are well known for it. Lumpiang sariwa is a fresh roll of vegetables and ubod (heart of palm) in a thin wrapper. Hopia is a pastry, and the old bakeries near Quiapo are famous for it.

This entry focuses on the food around Quiapo Church rather than on the church itself, which has its own entry. Hygiene and prices at the stalls are not consistent, and the market is hot and crowded, but there is a pleasure in queuing and eating among locals in the daytime. Because pickpocketing is frequent here, keep a close watch on your belongings, and we advise against going into the alleys alone after dark. After Quiapo, you might continue on foot to Intramuros or Binondo and compare other sides of old Manila.

There are palabok specialist stalls inside Quinta Market and under Quezon Bridge. A plate of rice noodles with shrimp-broth sauce, crushed chicharon and egg is the classic Quiapo lunch. The thickness of the sauce and the toppings differ from shop to shop, so the taste varies even under the same name. Some shops offer a special version topped with squid and lechon kawali, so look at the menu.

blocks.title: Sotanghon and pancit on Hidalgo Street

children.text: Eateries on Hidalgo Street serve sotanghon (glass-noodle soup) and stir-fried noodles. Each shop tastes different, so try small portions and compare.

blocks.title: Fresh rolls at Globe Lumpia House

children.text: Lumpiang sariwa, a roll of heart of palm and vegetables with a brown sauce, is described as costing about ₱40 each. It is a light Chinoy snack.

In the Muslim quarter you can try pastil (seasoned meat on rice wrapped in banana leaf) and Maranao dishes such as chicken piaparan. Pastil has been reported at around ₱10 each. Halal food uses no pork and is rich in spices and coconut, so if you are sensitive to heat, ask for it less spicy.
A hopia factory on Carlos Palanca Street is said to have been baking in a wood-fired oven since 1927. The two classic fillings are mung bean and pork.
Snack stalls selling fish balls, kwek-kwek (fried quail eggs) and isaw line the area around the church. They are good for a light bite as you walk.

blocks.title: Chinese-style ham and old Chinese restaurants

children.text: Near Quinta Market, a few Chinese-style ham shops and old Chinese-Filipino restaurants remain. Around Christmas they are crowded with people buying ham.

items.title: A half-day Quiapo food walk
items.subtitle: From the church to the market and the Muslim quarter

children.text: Get off at LRT-1 Carriedo Station and walk along Carriedo Street to Quiapo Church and Plaza Miranda. Enjoy the stalls and crowds on the way, and keep your belongings in front of you.
Around Plaza Miranda, whet your appetite with fish balls or kwek-kwek, then move on to the area under Quezon Bridge.
Have palabok for lunch in Quinta Market or at an eatery under Quezon Bridge. Popular shops run short of seats, so be ready to wait.
Look around the hopia and Chinese-style ham shops on Carlos Palanca Street and pick up something for dessert.
In the Muslim quarter on A. Bautista Street behind Hidalgo Street, taste pastil and sweet dodol. You can also look around the Golden Mosque.
Head back toward Carriedo while it is still light and take the LRT or a taxi onward.
Many markets and stalls wind down early in the afternoon, so we recommend starting before lunch. Opening hours differ from shop to shop, so confirm locally.

items.title: Linking old Manila's food districts
items.subtitle: Walking on from Quiapo to Binondo

children.text: See Quiapo Church and Plaza Miranda, and have palabok for lunch.
Take a taxi or jeepney to Binondo Chinatown and enjoy Chinese-Filipino snacks and tea.
Return to your hotel before dark.
The two districts are close enough to combine into a half-day plan, but do not overdo it given the heat and the crowds.
A taxi from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) varies greatly in time depending on traffic, and one guide puts the fare at around
. Beware of rip-off fares and check that the meter is used.
A ride-hailing app such as Grab lets you see the fare in advance, which is convenient.
Get off at LRT-1 Carriedo Station and walk along Carriedo Street toward Quiapo Church. It is about
10 minutes
on foot.
The area around the station is very crowded, so carry your bag in front and check your belongings on the exit stairs.
Carriedo Street is described as a little rough for first-time visitors, so go in the daytime.
A taxi to Quiapo Church from most parts of Manila is reported to cost about
. It varies with traffic.
Some city bus routes end at Quiapo, with stops near the church on Quezon Boulevard and under Carriedo Station.
Quiapo has many outdoor stalls, so the weather matters a lot. The November–May dry season is best for walking, but midday in March–May is very hot.

Every Friday, pilgrims flock to Quiapo Church and the area around it gets very crowded, and when the Black Nazarene procession is held on January 9 each year, the whole district is closed to traffic. At those times, avoid a food walk or finish early.

The liveliest time of day, with the widest choice of food, is between 10 AM and 2 PM. Later in the afternoon, more shops run out of ingredients or close and the alleys grow dark, so try to finish before sunset. When it rains, the covered stretch under Quezon Bridge is a good shelter, but the ground gets muddy.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Comfortable for walking, but crowded during the Christmas season and the January procession.
Finish your food walk in the morning and rest indoors at midday.
Stalls may close early or flood, so bring an umbrella.

items.label: Plate of palabok
items.note: Varies by shop and portion size

items.label: Taxi
items.note: About ₱200 within the city, about ₱300 from the airport according to a guide

Quiapo itself has few notable places to stay, and most visitors stay in Intramuros, Malate or Makati and come for a day. If the food walk is your goal, a hotel near an LRT-1 station is convenient.

It is easy to think of meals in three groups. For a simple lunch, palabok or sotanghon. For a light snack, lumpia and hopia. And for Islamic food, the halal eateries in the Muslim quarter. Remember that pork is not sold in Muslim areas and that alcohol is hard to find.

Drink only bottled water, and be selective about ice and raw food. Do not order too much at once; eating small portions is the safest approach. Shop names and hours change, so also check recent reviews on a map app.

If it is your first visit, you can also join a guided food walking tour. It is safer than walking alone, and moving between shops and ordering are much easier. If you go alone, mark just three points on your map, lunch, dessert and the Muslim quarter in that order, make one loop in the morning and leave early. Rather than trying to eat everything, pick one thing and taste it properly.
Pickpockets are common here, so carry your bag in front and do not hold your phone in your hand for long.
Prepare cash in small bills. Most stalls take cash only.
If a market vendor's price differs from others, compare shops and bargain.
We recommend eating before the afternoon, when some places run out of ingredients.
In the Muslim quarter, avoid revealing clothing and ask vendors before taking photos.
Fridays in front of the church and the days around January 9 are extremely crowded, so avoid them.
Snacks from the Muslim quarter such as pastil or dodol can be packed up and eaten at your hotel.
The market floors are wet and narrow, so wear closed shoes.
Rather than ordering everything at one shop, move between shops and share one plate at a time to taste more variety.
Quiapo is an area where pickpocketing never stops. Do not enter the alleys after dark, and leave valuables at your hotel.
Street food of uncertain hygiene can be hard on sensitive stomachs. Choose a stall where the cooking happens in front of you.
Check whether a taxi uses its meter, and if not, use a ride-hailing app such as Grab.
Carriedo Street and the area around the church have many beggars and touts. Decline firmly but politely.
Shop locations and hours differ between sources. Check a map app and recent reviews before you go.
Roads are closed on some days for events and pilgrimages, so check the latest notices.
The church is famous for the Black Nazarene statue and connects to the street-food area. It is within
5 minutes
on foot.
A food district called the oldest Chinatown in the world. It is about
10–20 minutes
away by taxi.
A Gothic church known for its steel structure, close to Quiapo.
A street of cheap wholesale markets where you can browse shopping and food together.
A former commercial center, good for an architectural stroll.
